Title: Who broke CI this time?
Description: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runners mean that when a job hangs, the first question is always the same: is it me or is it GitHub? So I built one page that answers it. runner-watch reads each runner's process tree and socket table through yeet's system graph, once a second, to show the whole fleet at a glance: who's busy, what step is stuck and on what, and whether the listener still has its long-poll open to GitHub. No agent inside the job, the runner software untouched, and the whole deploy is one service.toml.

Title: How reliable are confidence scores from language models?

We use the probability assigned to the chosen answer as its confidence score—the model’s estimate of how likely that answer is to be correct.

Title: I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere)
Description:
This video examines the amount of location information carried by inaudible background sounds, using the Doppler effect to locate a reference recording within ~100m, and only needing (in some cases) less 1-min of audio. This video raises awareness of these capabilities and closes by discussing preventative measures one could take.

Methodology: 
Aircraft position, altitude, and velocity data were sourced from ADS-B data and filtered in Python using ICAO type-code classification for propeller vs jet types. For each candidate location on a 200m grid, the closest point of approach (CPA) and sound propagation delay were computed from 3D slant distance, using a digital elevation model (DEM).

Doppler curve spectrogram measurements constrained each event's velocity and CPA slant distance. Candidates were then filtered by the 920-second offset between two flyovers, plus a silence constraint. The exact Doppler curve each candidate would hear was modelled, using emission-time radial velocity from interpolated ADS-B data. 

Modelled doppler curves were scored against the observed spectrogram using a locked two-event scoring method. This corrected for measurement error on CPA time & fundamental frequency, while preserving the purely physics-derived temporal offset between the two events.

The pipeline was repeated again for a single 1-min clip of known time, US-wide search, and again, successfully scored the true location 1st.

Lastly, preventative measures were assessed, including rationale behind why common signal processing fixes fail (high-pass filtering, drowning out, and phone call compression/noise reduction).

This video is an educational demonstration of acoustics, signal processing, and data analysis using publicly available data. No code or tools are being released.


Link to full recording: https://youtu.be/4CxVxuMVkMc

Title: The US election could turn the country into chaos
Description: Trump already tried to overturn one election he lost. On November 3, he’s likely to lose another one, badly. At this point it is obvious to almost everybody that the Republican Party, and thus Trump, is going to get smashed in the midterms. Chances are that both the House and the Senate will be flipped. A year ago, it was mostly unthinkable that the Democrats could flip the Senate. Although it would be a massive loss, even for a midterm, in this post I want to make the point that this is not just another election. Trump doesn’t like to lose I don’t think Trump would take this loss lightly, especially after a potential landslide. I think Trump will challenge, litigate and threaten to get the result of the election overturned, at least in key states. Some of the litigation has already started. When I mention this to folks, so far everyone replies with skepticism: they don’t think that could happen, or that it’s even possible. To me this is a clear example of normalcy bias, and it’s quite easy to show why: Trump has already tried to overturn an election that he lost, in 2020. To this day, he doesn’t admit that he lost that election, and neither do key members of his cabinet. That alone should have been a massive red flag against voting for him in 2024, but here we are anyway and it’s about to happen again1. There is speculation that the administration will try to influence the elections by using force, but as this excellent piece from Nate Silver’s newsletter describes, it may not even be possible to do at scale, although they might pull it off in a specific key race. Even if it doesn’t happen, the fact that we’re talking about it at all says a lot about how unstable things could get. Many people think that he doesn’t admit he lost because he genuinely believes he won. The case for unfitness is the same either way: either he ignored the popular vote to stay in power unlawfully, or he was delusional (or dumb) enough to reject a clear reality. ↩
